title: Middle powers search for room to maneuver after the APEC summit
lead: While the largest governments held headline-making talks, countries such as Canada looked for ways to diversify their economic and diplomatic relationships.
body: Reuters examined how nations that are not superpowers are responding to a world increasingly shaped by competition among Washington, Beijing and Moscow. New regional trade discussions and technology partnerships are part of an effort to avoid depending on any one partner too heavily.
These choices reflect a practical reality: a country can benefit from trade with a major economy while also worrying about supply chains, strategic autonomy and the stability of alliances.
why: Diversified relationships can give smaller and middle-sized economies more options when global politics changes suddenly.

title: US farm exporters see less benefit than hoped from Asia trade diplomacy
lead: Trade deals may make impressive diplomatic headlines, but farmers are watching whether agricultural orders and shipments actually increase.
body: A Reuters examination contrasted Donald Trump's positive account of Asian trade talks with the weaker results being felt in parts of US agriculture. Announcements and market access are only the beginning; exporters also need competitive prices, transport arrangements and dependable purchasers.
The mismatch illustrates why international agreements should be assessed through actual trade flows rather than declarations alone. For producers, the test is whether customers place orders.
why: Agricultural exports affect farmers, commodity supply chains and rural businesses far beyond trade negotiators.

title: Taiwan alerts Meta to suspected coordinated accounts before local elections
lead: Authorities in Taiwan said they had identified nearly 2,700 accounts that appeared linked to an effort to influence political discussion online.
body: Taiwanese officials described suspicious activity on Meta's Threads platform ahead of local elections on November 28. They said some accounts appeared to have been created in batches and that fabricated videos may have been used to amplify politically charged messages.

Meta said it had removed many accounts flagged by the government while disputing the characterization of some of their activity. The report highlights why allegations about information operations require careful investigation and responses from all parties.
why: Coordinated online activity can affect public confidence even when individual posts look ordinary.

title: A new migrant caravan moves through southern Mexico
lead: A group of around 300 migrants crossed into southern Mexico to join others moving north as political pressure on border policy increased.
body: People in the new group, most from Central America, joined a larger movement that had already divided into smaller groups. Participants described exhaustion and uncertainty about where they might find a safe place to live and work.

The journey unfolded amid US threats of additional tariffs if Mexico did not halt migrant movement. Mexican authorities said cases would be considered according to individuals' documentation and legal status.
why: Migration decisions involve human lives as well as complex national questions about borders, employment and legal protections.

title: White House order raises questions about congressional oversight of contractors
lead: A new executive order directing federal contractors to check with the White House over congressional inquiries drew scrutiny over access to information.
body: The measure was issued as Democratic lawmakers prepared to use oversight tools more extensively following election gains. Supporters of tighter coordination may see contractor inquiries as part of executive-branch management; critics question whether centralized clearance could weaken lawmakers' ability to obtain independent answers.

The broader dispute concerns the balance between executive authority and Congress's oversight responsibilities. Legal challenges and agency practice may determine how much the order changes in reality.
why: Access to contractor information can matter for spending oversight and the accountability of government programs.

title: Saudi security concerns deepen after a strike on a Riyadh tower
lead: An incident involving a tower linked to Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund added to concern about attacks on economic infrastructure.
body: Reuters reported damage to a building belonging to the Public Investment Fund in Riyadh on November 19. Saudi authorities referred to a missile threat and material damage, while sources cited by Reuters linked the incident to a projectile attributed to the Houthis; responsibility for that particular strike was not immediately claimed.

The wider region has faced repeated disruptions affecting transport, energy and commercial facilities. Investigators and authorities must establish details before specific responsibility can be treated as settled.
why: Security disruptions can affect economic confidence and the operation of infrastructure far beyond a single location.

title: China's housing downturn could extend into 2027, analysts say
lead: A Reuters survey suggests China's property market may continue struggling even if the pace of some price declines moderates.
body: Analysts surveyed by Reuters expected home prices to remain under pressure into 2027 amid large inventories and uncertain household incomes. Their forecasts reflected the difficulty of restoring confidence after years of financial stress in the real-estate sector.

Housing matters to China's broader economy because it touches construction, household wealth, local-government revenue and demand for materials. The forecasts are estimates, not certainties about future prices.
why: Changes in Chinese construction and consumer confidence can influence producers and trade partners across the world.

title: Record AI-chip profits fail to stop foreign selling in South Korea
lead: South Korea's biggest technology companies posted powerful earnings, yet overseas investors continued reducing exposure to its stock market.
body: Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix benefited from demand for memory chips used in artificial-intelligence systems. At the same time, Reuters reported a prolonged period of foreign selling and a sharp reversal in the KOSPI's earlier gains.

That mismatch highlights the difference between strong corporate results and investors' willingness to take market risk. Concerns about AI infrastructure spending and future regulation can affect share prices long before factories stop receiving orders.
why: The story shows how markets can weaken even when major companies are profitable.

title: Europe pushes for a stronger clean-energy signal at COP31
lead: EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra urged negotiators not to lose sight of the need to reduce emissions from fossil fuels.
body: At the summit in Turkey, Hoekstra argued that draft language was distracting delegations from the central work of moving toward cleaner energy. The intervention reflected disagreements about whether the global agreement should describe a transition away from oil, coal and gas more directly.

Negotiators had to balance ambition with the economic circumstances of nearly 200 participating governments. The disagreement was about both the timetable and the words countries were prepared to endorse.
why: An international message on energy investment can influence national plans even without a single global regulator.

title: AI-related selling sends US stock benchmarks sharply lower
lead: A sharp retreat in technology shares left major US stock indexes under pressure as investors questioned valuations and economic risks.
body: Reuters reported heavy losses across AI-linked companies, including a difficult week for Nvidia and a decline following Anthropic's much-discussed stock-market arrival. Investors also weighed interest-rate expectations, spending on data centers and investigations affecting the chip industry.

Large share-price movements do not necessarily mean that artificial-intelligence adoption has stopped. They show that financial markets can reassess how quickly anticipated future profits might appear.
why: Stock-market reversals can influence retirement portfolios, corporate funding and decisions about technology investment.
